issues.legal_issue: The statutory requirement to exhaust revenue appeals before bringing a civil suit does not bar a title suit between private parties.
material_facts: The parties had jointly purchased the property and later asserted competing rights to it.

A revenue appeal concerning the property was dismissed, and the party who brought it did not pursue a further revision before filing a civil suit seeking a declaration of title and a perpetual injunction.
The civil suit was between private parties and sought determination of rights in the property.
issues.conclusion: The civil suit between the private parties was maintainable, notwithstanding that the further revenue remedy had not been pursued.
issues.legal_principle: Section 11 of the Bombay Revenue Jurisdiction Act bars a suit against the Government concerning an act or omission of a Revenue Officer unless the plaintiff first exhausts the appeals available within the prescribed period; it does not bar a suit between private parties. Section 9 of the Code of Civil Procedure does not expressly or by necessary implication exclude civil jurisdiction over a suit based on title. Section 37 of the Bombay Land Revenue Code concerns land vesting in or belonging to the State and does not govern inter se claims of private parties. Mutation entries facilitate revenue collection and may evidence enjoyment, but do not create title, which must be established independently of those entries.

predicates.civil_suit_between_private_parties: The proceeding is a civil suit brought by one private party against another, rather than a suit against the Government.
predicates.seeks_determination_of_property_title: The plaintiff asks the civil court to determine title or other rights in property.

issues.definition: When a civil suit between private parties asks the court to determine property title, the suit is maintainable.

issues.legal_issue: An order restraining alienation of disputed property while a maintainable title suit is pending may be upheld.
material_facts: The plaintiff sought a declaration of title and a perpetual injunction concerning jointly purchased property over which the parties asserted competing rights.
The trial court refused an injunction, but the appellate court restrained the opposing party from alienating the property pending the suit, and the High Court left that order undisturbed.
The Supreme Court found no illegality in the High Court's order and noted that a purchaser during the litigation would take subject to its result.
issues.conclusion: The order restraining alienation pending the suit was upheld, and there was no ground to interfere with it.
issues.legal_principle: Section 52 of the Transfer of Property Act embodies the rule of lis pendens: a transfer during pending litigation does not defeat the rights determined in that litigation, and a purchaser takes subject to its result. The Court relied on that rule in upholding the restraint against alienation.

predicates.property_title_suit_pending: A civil suit seeking a determination of rights in property is pending.
predicates.disputed_property_may_be_transferred: A party to the dispute could transfer or alienate the property while the suit is pending.

issues.definition: When a property title suit is pending and the disputed property may be transferred, a restraint on alienation pending the suit is upheld.
